sections.h2: What should a Minnesota home seller know about the state first?
sections.html:
Minnesota is a large state with one dominant metro area and a long list of rural counties. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 5,830,405 residents, and the state spans 86,943 square miles across 87 counties.

More than 60 percent of residents, about 3.71 million people, live in the Minneapolis and Saint Paul metropolitan area. Duluth, Mankato, Moorhead, Rochester, and St. Cloud anchor the smaller metropolitan and micropolitan areas. Saint Paul is the capital, Minneapolis is the largest city, and the territory became the 32nd state on May 11, 1858.

The land itself varies. Roughly a third of the state is forest, the rest is mostly prairie and farmland, and the lake count is 11,842 lakes over 10 acres. Winters are cold and summers hot, with a growing season that runs from about 90 days in the far northeast to 160 days in the southeast. That range matters when a house needs a roof, drainage, or foundation work before a sale.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Minnesota homes?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts puts the median value of an owner-occupied Minnesota home at $329,300 for 2020 to 2024. Seventy-two percent of occupied homes are owned by the people living in them, and the median gross rent is $1,280.

sections.h2: How do Minnesota regions differ for sellers?
sections.html:
Each region has its own employers and housing stock, and that shapes who buys. The Twin Cities area holds the headquarters and manufacturing history: milling companies in Minneapolis, a medical device maker that began there in 1949, and a metropolitan planning body, the Metropolitan Council, created in 1967.

  • Rochester: the Mayo Clinic, founded there in 1864, is the state's largest private employer.
  • Duluth and the Iron Range: iron mining began in the Vermilion and Mesabi ranges in the 1880s, ore moved by rail to Duluth and Two Harbors, and taconite mining continues.
  • Southern and western Minnesota: farmland and small cities such as Mankato and Moorhead, where Moorhead recorded the state's high of 114 degrees in July 1936.
  • Northern Minnesota: forest and lakes, with Tower recording the state's low of minus 60 degrees in February 1996.

The state overview at Wikipedia covers the history behind these regions.

sections.h2: Which statewide rules shape a Minnesota property sale?
sections.html:
Several statutes apply in every county, and they are the starting point before county or city details come in.

  • Property tax: when a parcel's taxes top $100, half is due before May 16 and half before October 16, with a 2 percent penalty on homestead property and 4 percent on non-homestead property for a late half (Minn. Stat. 279.01).
  • Deed tax: a recorded deed carries a state tax of $1.65 for no consideration or $3,000 or less, and .0033 of net consideration above that (Minn. Stat. 287.21).
  • Seller disclosure: the disclosure rules exempt transfers to heirs or devisees, foreclosure transfers, court-ordered transfers, transfers to a tenant in possession, and transfers to a spouse, parent, grandparent, child, or grandchild (Minn. Stat. 513.54).
  • Foreclosure redemption: a mortgagor generally has six months after the sheriff's sale to redeem, and 12 months in listed cases such as land above 40 acres (Minn. Stat. 580.23).
  • Estate tax: a Minnesota return is required only when an estate's gross value exceeds $3,000,000 for deaths in 2020 or later, according to the Department of Revenue.

These figures can change with each legislative session, so confirm the current statute text before relying on a number.

sections.h2: How do Minnesota property tax penalties build up?
sections.html:
A late half starts with a 2 percent penalty on homestead property or 4 percent on non-homestead property. If the half is still unpaid on the first day of the next month, the same percentage is added again. Each later month through December adds 1 percent, and the total stops at 8 percent for homestead property and 12 percent for non-homestead property.

Two timing details matter at a closing. When a property tax statement is not postmarked before April 25, the first half is due 21 days after the postmark and the penalties follow that later date. A parcel with taxes of $100 or less owes the whole amount by the first due date. The county treasurer can tell a seller the current balance, and under section 279.01 the treasurer may take a payment of more or less than the exact installment and applies it to the oldest unpaid one first.

sections.h2: Where do Minnesota deeds and judgments get recorded?
sections.html:
Documents go to the county recorder for ordinary land and to the registrar of titles for registered land. Minn. Stat. 504B.291 uses exactly this split for eviction judgments, and the same two offices serve a buyer who needs to confirm what is recorded against a house.

Because Minnesota has 87 counties, each with its own recorder, treasurer, and assessor, the office that answers a question depends on the parcel's county. Ask the county treasurer for tax statements and payment status, the assessor for value and classification, and the recorder for deeds, liens, and judgments. A closing agent usually runs this search, but a seller with a probate house, a rental, or a back tax bill benefits from knowing which office holds each record.

sections.h2: Which Minnesota guide fits my situation?
sections.html:
The statewide pages on this site are organized by the problem a seller faces. Pick the one that matches yours, then move to the county or city page for local offices.

  • An inherited house or a death in the family: the estate tax guide covers the $3,000,000 filing level, the 13 to 16 percent rate, and the nine-month due date.
  • A tenant in the house: the eviction notice guide covers the 14-day nonpayment notice, and the eviction process guide covers the court steps after it.
  • Behind on the mortgage: the foreclosure rules begin with the six-month redemption period after the sheriff's sale.
  • A property tax bill or an appeal: the property tax guides cover payment dates and penalties, and the county guides name the local offices.
  • A sale in a specific town: the city pages tie local rules and neighborhoods to the process of selling fast.

The estate tax and eviction guides draw on the statutes and Department of Revenue pages cited above, so the figures match what the state publishes.

faqs.q: How many counties are there in Minnesota?
faqs.a: Eighty-seven. Each has its own recorder, treasurer, and assessor, so the office to call depends on where the house sits. The Twin Cities metro counties hold most of the state's people, and 40 of the 87 counties lost residents between 1980 and 2000.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Minnesota?
faqs.a: $329,300 for owner-occupied housing units from 2020 to 2024, according to Census QuickFacts. The same table gives a median gross rent of $1,280 and an owner-occupied rate of 72.2 percent. Local values vary widely from the state figure.

faqs.q: When are Minnesota property taxes due?
faqs.a: In two halves, before May 16 and before October 16, when a parcel's taxes exceed $100. A late half draws a 2 percent penalty on homestead property or 4 percent on non-homestead property, with more added if it stays unpaid into the next month.

faqs.q: How long does a homeowner have to redeem after a Minnesota foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: Six months after the sheriff's sale in most cases. Statute section 580.23 lists situations with 12 months, such as mortgages on land larger than 40 acres. Ask the county sheriff's office or an attorney which period applies to a specific mortgage.

faqs.q: Does Minnesota require a seller disclosure when an heir sells an inherited house?
faqs.a: Section 513.54 lists a transfer to heirs or devisees of a decedent among the exceptions to the seller disclosure rules. Ask the closing agent whether an exception fits the particular sale.
